claim: The occipital cortex of early blind individuals activates during speech processing.
source: The occipital cortex of early blind individuals (EB) activates during speech processing, challenging the notion of a hard-wired neurobiology of language.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that motivates the current study.

claim: Parieto-occipital regions in early blind individuals enhance their synchronization to acoustic fluctuations in human speech in the theta-range corresponding to syllabic rate, irrespective of speech intelligibility.
source: Here we demonstrate that parieto-occipital regions in EB enhance their synchronization to acoustic fluctuations in human speech in the theta-range (corresponding to syllabic rate), irrespective of speech intelligibility.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on MEG data analysis showing enhanced coherence in parieto-occipital regions.

claim: Enhanced synchronization to the intelligibility of speech was selectively observed in primary visual cortex in early blind individuals.
source: Crucially, enhanced synchronization to the intelligibility of speech was selectively observed in primary visual cortex in EB, suggesting that this region is at the interface between speech perception and comprehension.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the interaction analysis showing calcarine sulcus (V1) responds more to intelligible speech in EB.

claim: Early blind individuals showed overall enhanced functional connectivity between temporal and occipital cortices that are sensitive to speech intelligibility.
source: Moreover, EB showed overall enhanced functional connectivity between temporal and occipital cortices that are sensitive to speech intelligibility and altered directionality when compared to the sighted group.
evidence: This is based on phase-locking value analysis showing greater connectivity in EB versus SI.

claim: Early blind individuals showed altered directionality of connectivity between temporal and occipital cortices when compared to the sighted group.
source: Moreover, EB showed overall enhanced functional connectivity between temporal and occipital cortices that are sensitive to speech intelligibility and altered directionality when compared to the sighted group.
evidence: This is based on phase-slope index analysis showing different directional patterns between groups.

claim: The occipital cortex of the blind adopts an architecture that allows the tracking of speech material and does not fully abstract from the reorganized sensory inputs it receives.
source: These findings suggest that the occipital cortex of the blind adopts an architecture that allows the tracking of speech material, and therefore does not fully abstract from the reorganized sensory inputs it receives.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings that occipital cortex tracks speech envelope, suggesting sensory-level processing.

claim: The neurobiological organization of the human language system is often argued to be the result of innate constraints.
source: The consistency of this functional mapping across individuals and its presence early in development are remarkable, and often used to argue that the neurobiological organization of the human language system is the result of innate constraints (Dehaene-Lambertz et al., 2006; Berwick et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Strong nativist theories for linguistic innateness leave little room for plasticity due to experience.
source: Strong nativist theories for linguistic innateness leave little room for plasticity due to experience (Bates, 1999), suggesting that we should conceive 'the growth of language as analogous to the development of a bodily organ' (Chomsky, 1976, p.11).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bates (1999) and Chomsky (1976).

claim: Infants born with extensive damage to cortical regions typically involved in language processing may develop normal language abilities.
source: However, studies in infants born with extensive damage to cortical regions that are typically involved in language processing may develop normal language abilities, thereby demonstrating that the language network is subject to reorganization (Bates, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bates (2005).

claim: Primary and secondary 'visual' areas in congenitally blind individuals show functional selectivity to language.
source: Perhaps the most intriguing demonstrations to show that the neurobiology of language is susceptible to change due to experience come from studies showing functional selectivity to language in primary and secondary 'visual' areas in congenitally blind individuals (Röder et al., 2002; Burton, 2003; Amedi et al., 2004; Bedny et al., 2011; Arnaud et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Speech comprehension requires that the brain extracts meaning from the acoustic features of sounds.
source: Speech comprehension requires that the brain extracts meaning from the acoustic features of sounds (de Heer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Heer et al. (2017).

claim: Understanding spoken language relies on the ability to track the incoming acoustic signal in near real-time.
source: Because speech unfolds over time, understanding spoken language relies on the ability to track the incoming acoustic signal in near real-time (Peelle and Davis, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peelle and Davis (2012).

claim: Speech is a fluctuating acoustic signal that rhythmically excites neuronal populations in the brain.
source: Indeed, speech is a fluctuating acoustic signal that rhythmically excites neuronal populations in the brain (Poeppel et al., 2008; Gross et al., 2013; Peelle et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neuronal populations in auditory areas entrain to the acoustic fluctuations present in human speech around the syllabic rate.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that neuronal populations in auditory areas entrain to the acoustic fluctuations that are present in human speech around the syllabic rate (Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Kayser et al., 2009; Szymanski et al., 2011; Zoefel and VanRullen, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Entrainment reflects a key mechanism underlying hearing by facilitating the parsing of individual syllables through adjusting the sensory gain relative to fluctuations in the acoustic energy.
source: It has therefore been suggested that entrainment reflects a key mechanism underlying hearing by facilitating the parsing of individual syllables through adjusting the sensory gain relative to fluctuations in the acoustic energy (Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Peelle and Davis, 2012; Ding and Simon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some regions that track the specific acoustic rhythm of speech are sensitive to speech intelligibility.
source: Crucially, because some regions that track the specific acoustic rhythm of speech are sensitive to speech intelligibility, neural synchronization is not only driven by changes in the acoustic cue of the auditory stimuli, but also reflects cortical encoding and processing of the auditory signal (Peelle et al., 2013; Ding and Simon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peelle et al. (2013) and Ding and Simon (2014).

claim: Neural synchronization is not only driven by changes in the acoustic cue of the auditory stimuli, but also reflects cortical encoding and processing of the auditory signal.
source: Crucially, because some regions that track the specific acoustic rhythm of speech are sensitive to speech intelligibility, neural synchronization is not only driven by changes in the acoustic cue of the auditory stimuli, but also reflects cortical encoding and processing of the auditory signal (Peelle et al., 2013; Ding and Simon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peelle et al. (2013) and Ding and Simon (2014).

claim: Speech tracking is an invaluable tool to probe regions that interface speech perception and comprehension.
source: Speech tracking is therefore an invaluable tool to probe regions that interface speech perception and comprehension (Poeppel et al., 2008; Gross et al., 2013; Peelle et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Intelligibility had a significant effect on story comprehension.
source: Intelligibility had a significant effect on story comprehension (χ(2)=110.7, p<0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data using linear mixed-effects models.

claim: The effect of blindness on story comprehension was non-significant.
source: The effect of blindness and the interaction between intelligibility and blindness were non-significant (χ(1)=1.14, p=0.286 and χ(2)=0.24, p=0.889).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The interaction between intelligibility and blindness on story comprehension was non-significant.
source: The effect of blindness and the interaction between intelligibility and blindness were non-significant (χ(1)=1.14, p=0.286 and χ(2)=0.24, p=0.889).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Speech comprehension was stronger in the natural and 8-channel condition versus the 1-channel condition.
source: Orthogonal contrasts demonstrated that speech comprehension was stronger in the nat and 8-channel condition versus the 1-channel condition (b = 0.78, t(62)=14.43, p<0.001, r = 0.88).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was no difference in speech comprehension between the natural and the 8-channel condition.
source: There was no difference between the nat and the 8-channel condition (b = 0.02, t(62)=1.39, p=0.17).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Speech intelligibility was reduced in the 1-channel vocoded condition but not the 8-channel vocoded condition.
source: Thus, speech intelligibility was reduced in the 1-channel, but not the 8-channel vocoded condition (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on behavioral comprehension data and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is no evidence for a potential difference in comprehension, attention or motivation between early blind and sighted groups.
source: The lack of effect for the factor blindness suggests that there is no evidence for a potential difference in comprehension, attention or motivation between groups.
evidence: This is inferred from the non-significant effect of blindness on behavioral performance.

claim: The overall coherence spectrum between the amplitude envelope of speech and the MEG signal was maximal over temporal sensors between 6 Hz and 7 Hz.
source: The overall coherence spectrum, which highlights the relationship between the amplitude envelope of speech and the signal recorded from the brain, was maximal over temporal sensors between 6 Hz and 7 Hz (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on MEG coherence analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The peak coherence frequency in the current study is slightly higher than those reported in previous studies.
source: The peak in the current study is slightly higher than those reported in previous studies (Gross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature cited.

claim: The difference in syllabic rate between English (~6.2 Hz) and Italian (~7 Hz) likely explains the shift in peak coherence frequency.
source: A likely explanation for this shift is the difference in syllabic rate between English (~6.2 Hz), used in previous studies, and Italian (~7 Hz) (Pellegrino et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on known syllabic rates and citation to Pellegrino et al. (2011).

claim: The syllabic rate is the main carrier of amplitude fluctuations in speech.
source: The syllabic rate is the main carrier of amplitude fluctuations in speech, and thus is most prone to reset oscillatory activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about speech processing.

claim: Source-reconstructed coherence was strongest across groups and conditions in bilateral temporal lobes, including primary auditory cortex.
source: The source-reconstructed coherence at the frequency-range of interest confirmed that cerebro-acoustic coherence was strongest across groups and conditions in bilateral temporal lobes, including primary auditory cortex. (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on source reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Synchronization to the envelope of speech was stronger in right superior and middle temporal cortex when participants had access to the content of the story.
source: The resulting statistical map (Figure 1G, p<0.05, FWE-corrected) revealed a cluster in right superior and middle temporal cortex (STG, MTG), where synchronization to the envelope of speech was stronger when participants had access to the content of the story.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing intelligible versus non-intelligible conditions, shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The effect of intelligibility on the sensory response suggests an interface between acoustic speech processing and comprehension in STG that is present in both groups.
source: In other words, the effect of intelligibility on the sensory response (coherence with the speech envelope) suggests an interface between acoustic speech processing and comprehension in STG that is present in both groups.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing intelligibility effects in STG.

claim: Enhanced coherence in early blind versus sighted individuals was observed in parieto-occipital cortex along the medial wall, centered on bilateral Precuneus.
source: The statistical maps (Figure 1H, p<0.05, FWE-corrected) revealed enhanced coherence in EB versus SI in parieto-occipital cortex along the medial wall, centered on bilateral Precuneus, branching more extensively into the right hemisphere (see Table 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing EB and SI groups, shown in Figure 1H and Table 2.

claim: Neuronal populations in blind parieto-occipital cortex show enhanced synchronization to the acoustic speech signal.
source: This main effect of group highlights that neuronal populations in blind parieto-occipital cortex show enhanced synchronization to the acoustic speech signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the group difference in coherence.

claim: Blind participants show a stronger sensitivity to the sensory properties of the external speech stimulus in parieto-occipital cortex.
source: That is, blind participants show a stronger sensitivity to the sensory properties of the external speech stimulus at this level.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the enhanced coherence in EB.

claim: A significant effect of the interaction between blindness and intelligibility was observed in right calcarine sulcus.
source: A significant effect of the interaction between blindness and intelligibility [(natEB – 1-channelEB) – (natSI – 1-channelSI)] was observed in right calcarine sulcus.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the interaction effect.

claim: Intelligible speech selectively engages the area around the right calcarine sulcus in the blind versus the sighted.
source: This shows that intelligible speech selectively engages the area around the right calcarine sulcus in the blind versus the sighted.
evidence: This is based on the interaction analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The region corresponding to right 'visual' cortex showed enhanced sensitivity to intelligible speech in early blind versus sighted individuals.
source: Specifically, the region corresponding to right 'visual' cortex showed enhanced sensitivity to intelligible speech in EB versus SI (p<0.05, FWE-corrected).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the interaction effect.

claim: The analysis contrasting the two intelligible conditions (natural and 8-channel) did not yield a significant effect in the early blind.
source: However, the analysis contrasting the two intelligible conditions (nat and 8-channel) did not yield a significant effect in the EB, suggesting that the low-level degrading of the stimulus alone does not drive the effect, but rather the intelligibility of the speech segment.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing the two intelligible conditions.

claim: Low-level degrading of the stimulus alone does not drive the effect in calcarine sulcus, but rather the intelligibility of the speech segment.
source: However, the analysis contrasting the two intelligible conditions (nat and 8-channel) did not yield a significant effect in the EB, suggesting that the low-level degrading of the stimulus alone does not drive the effect, but rather the intelligibility of the speech segment.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of difference between natural and 8-channel conditions.

claim: Coherence was stronger during the intelligible condition for early blind versus sighted individuals.
source: Follow-up post hoc comparisons between the two groups revealed that coherence was stronger during the intelligible condition for EB versus SI (t[30] = 3.09, p=0.004), but not during the unintelligible condition (t[30] = –1.08, p=0.29).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical comparisons.

claim: Coherence during the unintelligible condition did not differ between early blind and sighted individuals.
source: Follow-up post hoc comparisons between the two groups revealed that coherence was stronger during the intelligible condition for EB versus SI (t[30] = 3.09, p=0.004), but not during the unintelligible condition (t[30] = –1.08, p=0.29).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical comparisons.

claim: A group difference between early blind and sighted individuals across conditions was not observed in the calcarine region.
source: A group difference between EB and SI across conditions was not observed in the calcarine region (t[30] = 1.1, p=0.28).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison.

claim: The lack of an overall group effect in calcarine sulcus suggests that there is not a simple enhanced sensory response to speech in the blind.
source: The lack of an overall group effect in calcarine sulcus suggests that there is not a simple enhanced sensory response to speech in the blind.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of main effect of group in calcarine sulcus.

claim: The response in calcarine sulcus only differed between the two groups when speech was intelligible.
source: Rather, the response in calcarine sulcus only differed between the two groups when speech was intelligible.
evidence: This is based on the interaction effect and post-hoc comparisons.

claim: Overall coherence with the speech envelope was equally high in early blind and sighted individuals.
source: While overall coherence with the speech envelope was equally high in EB and SI, the blind population showed significantly higher coherence in the intelligible speech condition than did the sighted, who showed higher cerebro-acoustic coherence in the unintelligible condition (1-Chan).
evidence: This is based on the pattern of results from the interaction analysis.

claim: The blind population showed significantly higher coherence in the intelligible speech condition than did the sighted.
source: While overall coherence with the speech envelope was equally high in EB and SI, the blind population showed significantly higher coherence in the intelligible speech condition than did the sighted, who showed higher cerebro-acoustic coherence in the unintelligible condition (1-Chan).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc comparisons.

claim: Sighted individuals showed higher cerebro-acoustic coherence in the unintelligible condition.
source: While overall coherence with the speech envelope was equally high in EB and SI, the blind population showed significantly higher coherence in the intelligible speech condition than did the sighted, who showed higher cerebro-acoustic coherence in the unintelligible condition (1-Chan).
evidence: This is based on the pattern of results from the interaction analysis.

claim: The more adverse the listening condition, the more the visual cortex is entrained to the visual speech signal when presented together with varying levels of acoustic noise.
source: The latter is reminiscent of the fact that the more adverse the listening condition (low signal-to-noise ratio or audiovisual incongruence), the more the visual cortex is entrained to the visual speech signal of actual acoustic speech when presented together with varying levels of acoustic noise (Park et al., 2016; Giordano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Park et al. (2016) and Giordano et al. (2017).

claim: Giordano et al. (2017) showed an increase of directed connectivity between superior frontal regions and visual cortex under the most challenging conditions.
source: Moreover, Giordano et al. (2017) showed an increase of directed connectivity between superior frontal regions and visual cortex under the most challenging (acoustic noise and uninformative visual cues) conditions, again suggesting a link between the reorganization observed in the occipital cortex of blind individuals and typical multisensory pathways involving the occipital cortex in audio-visual speech processing (Kayser et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Giordano et al. (2017).

claim: Visual deprivation since birth triggers a functional reorganization of the calcarine region that can dynamically interact with the intelligibility of the speech signal.
source: Visual deprivation since birth, however, triggers a functional reorganization of the calcarine region that can then dynamically interact with the intelligibility of the speech signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings showing intelligibility-dependent responses in calcarine sulcus of EB.

claim: A main effect was observed only for blindness on functional connectivity between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus.
source: A main effect was observed only for blindness (χ[1] = 4.32, p=0.038) and was caused by greater connectivity for EB versus SI (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis of phase-locking values.

claim: Greater connectivity between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus was observed for early blind versus sighted individuals.
source: A main effect was observed only for blindness (χ[1] = 4.32, p=0.038) and was caused by greater connectivity for EB versus SI (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The main effects of intelligibility and of the interaction between intelligibility and blindness on functional connectivity were non-significant.
source: The main effects of intelligibility and of the interaction between intelligibility and blindness were non-significant (p=0.241 and p=0.716, respectively).
evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis.

claim: Only the main effect of blindness was significant on the directional information flow between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus.
source: Here, only the main effect of blindness was significant (χ[1] = 4.54, p=0.033), indicating that the directional information flow differs between groups.
evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis of phase-slope index.

claim: The directional information flow between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus differs between early blind and sighted groups.
source: Here, only the main effect of blindness was significant (χ[1] = 4.54, p=0.033), indicating that the directional information flow differs between groups.
evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis of phase-slope index.

claim: The effect of intelligibility on directional information flow was non-significant.
source: The effect of intelligibility and the interaction between intelligibility and blindness were both non-significant (p=0.51 and p=0.377, respectively).
evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis.

claim: The interaction between intelligibility and blindness on directional information flow was non-significant.
source: The effect of intelligibility and the interaction between intelligibility and blindness were both non-significant (p=0.51 and p=0.377, respectively).
evidence: This is based on linear mixed-effects model analysis.

claim: Sighted individuals showed a significant direction bias from calcarine sulcus to superior temporal gyrus.
source: Follow-up post-hoc one-sample t-tests on the phase slope estimates for each group individually revealed a significant direction bias from CS to STG for SI (t[14] = –2.22, p=0.044).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc one-sample t-tests on phase-slope index.

claim: No directional bias was found for early blind individuals.
source: No directional bias was found for EB (t[16] = 0.74, p=0.47).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc one-sample t-tests on phase-slope index.

claim: Calcarine sulcus projects predominantly to superior temporal gyrus in sighted individuals.
source: As depicted in Figure 2C–D, these results suggest that CS projects predominantly to STG in SI, whereas in EB, this interaction is more balanced and trending in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is inferred from the phase-slope index results shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: In early blind individuals, the interaction between calcarine sulcus and superior temporal gyrus is more balanced and trending in the opposite direction compared to sighted individuals.
source: As depicted in Figure 2C–D, these results suggest that CS projects predominantly to STG in SI, whereas in EB, this interaction is more balanced and trending in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is inferred from the phase-slope index results shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The region around the Precuneus/Cuneus area is involved in low-level processing of acoustic information alone.
source: That is, the region around the Precuneus/Cuneus area seems to be involved in low-level processing of acoustic information alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that this region shows enhanced synchronization irrespective of intelligibility.

claim: The Precuneus/Cuneus area enhances its response to auditory information after early, but not late, visual deprivation.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that this area enhances its response to auditory information after early, but not late, visual deprivation (Collignon et al., 2013) and maintains this elevated response to sound even after sight-restoration early in life (Collignon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Collignon et al. (2013) and Collignon et al. (2015).

claim: The Precuneus/Cuneus area maintains elevated response to sound even after sight-restoration early in life.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that this area enhances its response to auditory information after early, but not late, visual deprivation (Collignon et al., 2013) and maintains this elevated response to sound even after sight-restoration early in life (Collignon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Collignon et al. (2015).

claim: Previous studies did not find that the Precuneus/Cuneus area's crossmodal response was related to a specific cognitive function, but rather pointed to a more general response to sounds.
source: These studies did not find that this crossmodal response was related to a specific cognitive function, but rather pointed to a more general response to sounds (Collignon et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Collignon et al. (2013, 2015).

claim: The Precuneus/Cuneus area is capable of parsing complex temporal patterns in sounds but is insensitive to the intelligibility of speech.
source: Interestingly, the current data suggest that this area is capable of parsing complex temporal patterns in sounds but is insensitive to the intelligibility of speech, again suggesting a more general role in sound processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the current study's findings showing enhanced synchronization irrespective of intelligibility.

claim: The pattern of local encoding in early blind individuals was accompanied by enhanced occipito-temporal connectivity during speech comprehension as compared to sighted individuals.
source: This pattern of local encoding was accompanied by enhanced occipito-temporal connectivity during speech comprehension in EB as compared to SI.
evidence: This is based on the connectivity analysis results.

claim: Sighted individuals show the expected feed-forward projections from occipital to temporal regions.
source: SI show the expected feed-forward projections from occipital to temporal regions (Lamme et al., 1998), whereas EB show a more balanced connectivity profile, trending towards the reverse temporal to occipital direction (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on phase-slope index analysis and citation to Lamme et al. (1998).

claim: Early blind individuals show a more balanced connectivity profile between occipital and temporal regions, trending towards the reverse temporal to occipital direction.
source: SI show the expected feed-forward projections from occipital to temporal regions (Lamme et al., 1998), whereas EB show a more balanced connectivity profile, trending towards the reverse temporal to occipital direction (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on phase-slope index analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The findings support the idea of a reverse hierarchical model of the occipital cortex in early blind individuals.
source: These findings support the idea of a reverse hierarchical model (Büchel, 2003) of the occipital cortex in EB, where the regions typically coding for 'low-level' visual features in the sighted (e.g. visual contrast or orientation) participate in higher-level function (e.g. speech intelligibility).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to Büchel (2003).

claim: In a reverse hierarchical model, regions typically coding for 'low-level' visual features in the sighted participate in higher-level function in early blind individuals.
source: These findings support the idea of a reverse hierarchical model (Büchel, 2003) of the occipital cortex in EB, where the regions typically coding for 'low-level' visual features in the sighted (e.g. visual contrast or orientation) participate in higher-level function (e.g. speech intelligibility).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citation to Büchel (2003).

claim: Previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of early blind people during Braille reading.
source: Indeed, previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of EB people during Braille reading (Sadato et al., 1996; Burton et al., 2002, 2012), verbal memory and verb generation tasks (Amedi et al., 2003), and during auditory language-related processing (Bedny et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of early blind people during verbal memory and verb generation tasks.
source: Indeed, previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of EB people during Braille reading (Sadato et al., 1996; Burton et al., 2002, 2012), verbal memory and verb generation tasks (Amedi et al., 2003), and during auditory language-related processing (Bedny et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Amedi et al. (2003).

claim: Previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of early blind people during auditory language-related processing.
source: Indeed, previous studies have found increased activity in the primary 'visual' cortex of EB people during Braille reading (Sadato et al., 1996; Burton et al., 2002, 2012), verbal memory and verb generation tasks (Amedi et al., 2003), and during auditory language-related processing (Bedny et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bedny et al. (2011).

claim: Activity in primary occipital regions in early blind people is stronger in a semantic versus a phonologic task.
source: In line with our results, activity in primary occipital regions in EB people is stronger in a semantic versus a phonologic task (Burton et al., 2003), and vary as a function of syntactic and semantic complexity (Röder et al., 2002; Bedny et al., 2011; Lane et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burton et al. (2003).

claim: Activity in primary occipital regions in early blind people varies as a function of syntactic and semantic complexity.
source: In line with our results, activity in primary occipital regions in EB people is stronger in a semantic versus a phonologic task (Burton et al., 2003), and vary as a function of syntactic and semantic complexity (Röder et al., 2002; Bedny et al., 2011; Lane et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Röder et al. (2002), Bedny et al. (2011), and Lane et al. (2015).

claim: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation over the occipital pole induces more semantic errors than phonologic errors in a verb-generation task in early blind people.
source: Moreover, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the occipital pole induces more semantic errors than phonologic errors in a verb-generation task in EB people (Amedi et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Amedi et al. (2003).

claim: The results clearly suggest that the involvement of the occipital pole for language is not fully abstracted from sensory inputs.
source: As we show that occipital regions entrain to the envelope of speech and are enhanced by its intelligibility, our results clearly suggest that the involvement of the occipital pole for language is not fully abstracted from sensory inputs as previously suggested (Bedny, 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in contrast to previous suggestions.

claim: The role of the occipital cortex in tracking the flow of speech in early blind people may constitute an adaptive strategy to boost perceptual sensitivity at informational peaks in language.
source: The role of the occipital cortex in tracking the flow of speech in EB people may constitute an adaptive strategy to boost perceptual sensitivity at informational peaks in language.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Language is not the only cognitive process that selectively activates the occipital cortex of early blind people.
source: Although language is not the only cognitive process that selectively activates the occipital cortex of EB people, it is arguably one of the most puzzling.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Reorganization of other processes such as auditory motion perception and tactile object recognition appears to follow the topography of the functionally equivalent visual processes in the sighted brain.
source: The reason is that reorganization of other processes, such as auditory motion perception and tactile object recognition, appears to follow the topography of the functionally equivalent visual processes in the sighted brain (Ricciardi et al., 2007a; Amedi et al., 2010; Dormal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ricciardi et al. (2007a), Amedi et al. (2010), and Dormal et al. (2016).

claim: The hMT+/V5 complex, which is typically involved in visual motion in the sighted, selectively processes auditory motion in blind people.
source: For example, the hMT+/V5 complex, which is typically involved in visual motion in the sighted, selectively processes auditory (Poirier et al., 2006; Dormal et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2016) or tactile (Ricciardi et al., 2007b) motion in blind people.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Poirier et al. (2006), Dormal et al. (2016), and Jiang et al. (2016).

claim: The hMT+/V5 complex, which is typically involved in visual motion in the sighted, selectively processes tactile motion in blind people.
source: For example, the hMT+/V5 complex, which is typically involved in visual motion in the sighted, selectively processes auditory (Poirier et al., 2006; Dormal et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2016) or tactile (Ricciardi et al., 2007b) motion in blind people.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ricciardi et al. (2007b).

claim: The recruitment of occipital cortex for language in blind people is striking in light of the cognitive and evolutionary differences between vision and language.
source: However, in the case of language, such recruitment is striking in light of the cognitive and evolutionary differences between vision and language (Bedny et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bedny et al. (2011).

claim: It has been proposed that at birth, human cortical areas are cognitively pluripotent: capable of assuming a broad range of unrelated cognitive functions.
source: This led to the proposal that, at birth, human cortical areas are cognitively pluripotent: capable of assuming a broad range of unrelated cognitive functions (Bedny, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bedny (2017).

claim: The cognitive pluripotency argument resides on the presupposition that language has no computational relation with vision.
source: However, this argument resides on the presupposition that language has no computational relation with vision.
evidence: This is an inference about the assumptions underlying the pluripotency argument.

claim: Rhythmic information in speech has a well-known language-related surrogate in the visual domain: lip movements.
source: But does this proposition tally with what we know about the relationship between the visual system and the classical language network? Rhythmic information in speech has a well-known language-related surrogate in the visual domain: lip movements (Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift, 2012; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift (2012) and Park et al. (2016).

claim: Both acoustic and visual speech signals exhibit rhythmic temporal patterns at prosodic and syllabic rates.
source: Indeed, both acoustic and visual speech signals exhibit rhythmic temporal patterns at prosodic and syllabic rates (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009; Schwartz and Savariaux, 2014; Giordano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chandrasekaran et al. (2009), Schwartz and Savariaux (2014), and Giordano et al. (2017).

claim: The perception of lip kinematics that are naturally linked to amplitude fluctuations in speech serves as an important vehicle for the everyday use of language.
source: The perception of lip kinematics that are naturally linked to amplitude fluctuations in speech serves as an important vehicle for the everyday use of language (Kuhl and Meltzoff, 1982; Weikum et al., 2007; Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift, 2012) and helps language understanding, particularly in noisy conditions (Ross et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kuhl and Meltzoff (1982), Weikum et al. (2007), Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift (2012), and Ross et al. (2007).

claim: Lip reading helps language understanding, particularly in noisy conditions.
source: The perception of lip kinematics that are naturally linked to amplitude fluctuations in speech serves as an important vehicle for the everyday use of language (Kuhl and Meltzoff, 1982; Weikum et al., 2007; Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift, 2012) and helps language understanding, particularly in noisy conditions (Ross et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ross et al. (2007).

claim: Reading lips in the absence of any sound activates both primary and association auditory regions overlapping with regions that are active during the actual perception of spoken words.
source: Indeed, reading lips in the absence of any sound activates both primary and association auditory regions overlapping with regions that are active during the actual perception of spoken words (Calvert et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Calvert et al. (1997).

claim: The synchronicity between auditory and visual speech entrains rhythmic activity in the observer's primary auditory and visual regions.
source: The synchronicity between auditory and visual speech entrains rhythmic activity in the observer's primary auditory and visual regions, and facilitates perception by aligning neural excitability with acoustic or visual speech features (Schroeder et al., 2008; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Mesgarani and Chang, 2012; Peelle and Davis, 2012; van Wassenhove, 2013; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013b; Park et al., 2016; Giordano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The synchronicity between auditory and visual speech facilitates perception by aligning neural excitability with acoustic or visual speech features.
source: The synchronicity between auditory and visual speech entrains rhythmic activity in the observer's primary auditory and visual regions, and facilitates perception by aligning neural excitability with acoustic or visual speech features (Schroeder et al., 2008; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Mesgarani and Chang, 2012; Peelle and Davis, 2012; van Wassenhove, 2013; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013b; Park et al., 2016; Giordano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Both the auditory and the visual components of speech are processed together at the earliest level possible in neural circuitry, based on the shared slow temporal modulations present across modalities.
source: These results strongly suggest that both the auditory and the visual components of speech are processed together at the earliest level possible in neural circuitry, based on the shared slow temporal modulations (around 2–7 Hz range) present across modalities (Chandrasekaran et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chandrasekaran et al. (2009).

claim: Neuronal populations in visual cortex follow the temporal dynamics of lip movements in sighted individuals, similar to the way in which temporal regions follow the acoustic and visual fluctuations of speech.
source: Corroborating this idea, it has been demonstrated that neuronal populations in visual cortex follow the temporal dynamics of lip movements in sighted individuals, similar to the way in which temporal regions follow the acoustic and visual fluctuations of speech (Luo et al., 2010; Zion Golumbic et al., 2013a; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luo et al. (2010), Zion Golumbic et al. (2013a), and Park et al. (2016).

claim: Occipital cortex in the sighted shows enhanced lip tracking when attention is directed to speech content.
source: Similar to temporal cortex, occipital cortex in the sighted also shows enhanced lip tracking when attention is directed to speech content.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous research.

claim: A basic oscillatory architecture for tracking the dynamic aspects of visual-speech in occipital cortex exists even in sighted individuals.
source: This result highlights the fact that a basic oscillatory architecture for tracking the dynamic aspects of (visual-) speech in occipital cortex exists even in sighted individuals.
evidence: This is inferred from the evidence of lip tracking in occipital cortex of sighted individuals.

claim: Audiovisual integration of the temporal dynamics of speech has been suggested to play a key role when learning speech early in life.
source: Importantly, audiovisual integration of the temporal dynamics of speech has been suggested to play a key role when learning speech early in life: young infants detect, match, and integrate the auditory and visual temporal coherence of speech (Kuhl and Meltzoff, 1982; Rosenblum et al., 1997; Lewkowicz, 2000, 2010; Brookes et al., 2001; Patterson and Werker, 2003; Lewkowicz and Ghazanfar, 2006; Kushnerenko et al., 2008; Bristow et al., 2009; Pons et al., 2009; Vouloumanos et al., 2009; Lewkowicz et al., 2010; Nath et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Young infants detect, match, and integrate the auditory and visual temporal coherence of speech.
source: Importantly, audiovisual integration of the temporal dynamics of speech has been suggested to play a key role when learning speech early in life: young infants detect, match, and integrate the auditory and visual temporal coherence of speech (Kuhl and Meltzoff, 1982; Rosenblum et al., 1997; Lewkowicz, 2000, 2010; Brookes et al., 2001; Patterson and Werker, 2003; Lewkowicz and Ghazanfar, 2006; Kushnerenko et al., 2008; Bristow et al., 2009; Pons et al., 2009; Vouloumanos et al., 2009; Lewkowicz et al., 2010; Nath et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Young infants between 4 and 6 months of age can detect their native language from lip movements only.
source: For instance, young infants between 4 and 6 months of age can detect their native language from lip movements only (Weikum et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weikum et al. (2007).

claim: Around 4 to 6 months of age, children detect synchrony between lip movements and speech sounds, and distribute more attention towards the mouth than towards the eyes.
source: Around the same period, children detect synchrony between lip movements and speech sounds, and distribute more attention towards the mouth than towards the eyes (Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift (2012).

claim: Linking what they hear to the lip movements may provide young infants with a stepping-stone towards language production.
source: Linking what they hear to the lip movements may provide young infants with a stepping-stone towards language production (Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lewkowicz and Hansen-Tift (2012).

claim: Infants aged 10 weeks already exhibit a McGurk effect.
source: Moreover, infants aged 10 weeks already exhibit a McGurk effect, again highlighting the early multisensory nature of speech perception (Rosenblum et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rosenblum et al. (1997).

claim: An audio-visual link between observing lip movements and hearing speech sounds is present at very early developmental stages, potentially from birth.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that an audio-visual link between observing lip movements and hearing speech sounds is present at very early developmental stages, potentially from birth, which helps infants acquire their first language.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence about early audiovisual integration in infants.

claim: The audio-visual link between observing lip movements and hearing speech sounds helps infants acquire their first language.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that an audio-visual link between observing lip movements and hearing speech sounds is present at very early developmental stages, potentially from birth, which helps infants acquire their first language.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence about early audiovisual integration in infants.

claim: The current results may support the biased connectivity hypothesis of cross-modal reorganization.
source: In line with these prior studies, the current results may support the biased connectivity hypothesis of cross-modal reorganization (Reich et al., 2011; Hannagan et al., 2015; Striem-Amit et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with citations to Reich et al. (2011), Hannagan et al. (2015), and Striem-Amit et al. (2015).

claim: Reorganization in blind occipital cortex may be constrained by functional pathways to other sensory and cognitive systems that are also present in sighted individuals.
source: Indeed, it has been argued that reorganization in blind occipital cortex may be constrained by functional pathways to other sensory and cognitive systems that are also present in sighted individuals (Elman et al., 1996; Hannagan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Elman et al. (1996) and Hannagan et al. (2015).

claim: The biased connectivity hypothesis may explain the overlap in functional specialization between blind and sighted individuals.
source: This hypothesis may explain the overlap in functional specialization between blind and sighted individuals (Collignon et al., 2011; Dormal et al., 2016; He et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2016; Peelen et al., 2013; Pietrini et al., 2004; Weeks et al., 2000; Poirier et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sensitivity to acoustic dynamics of intelligible speech in blind occipital cortex could arise from pre-existing occipito-temporal pathways connecting the auditory and visual system that are particularly important for the early developmental stages of language acquisition.
source: In our experiment, sensitivity to acoustic dynamics of intelligible speech in blind occipital cortex could arise from pre-existing occipito-temporal pathways connecting the auditory and visual system that are particularly important for the early developmental stages of language acquisition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism underlying the findings.

claim: The reorganization of the predisposed pathway to process language content would explain how language-selective response may appear in blind children as young as 3 years old.
source: In fact, the reorganization of this potentially predisposed pathway to process language content would explain how language-selective response may appear in blind children as young as 3 years old (Bedny et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the biased connectivity hypothesis and citation to Bedny et al. (2015).

claim: Previous studies have suggested that language processing in the occipital cortex arises through top-down projections from frontal regions typically associated with the classical language network.
source: Previous studies have suggested that language processing in the occipital cortex arises through top-down projections from frontal regions typically associated with the classical language network (Bedny et al., 2011; Deen et al., 2015), and that the representational content is symbolic and abstract rather than sensory (Bedny, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bedny et al. (2011), Deen et al. (2015), and Bedny (2017).

claim: Previous studies have suggested that the representational content in occipital cortex during language processing is symbolic and abstract rather than sensory.
source: Previous studies have suggested that language processing in the occipital cortex arises through top-down projections from frontal regions typically associated with the classical language network (Bedny et al., 2011; Deen et al., 2015), and that the representational content is symbolic and abstract rather than sensory (Bedny, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bedny (2017).

claim: The current results contrast with the view that occipital involvement in speech processing is abstracted from sensory input and purely reflects higher-level operations.
source: Our results contrast with this view by showing that neuronal populations in (peri-)calcarine cortex align to the temporal dynamics of intelligible speech, and are functionally connected to areas sensitive to auditory information in temporal cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in contrast to previous views.

claim: Neuronal populations in peri-calcarine cortex align to the temporal dynamics of intelligible speech.
source: Our results contrast with this view by showing that neuronal populations in (peri-)calcarine cortex align to the temporal dynamics of intelligible speech, and are functionally connected to areas sensitive to auditory information in temporal cortex.
evidence: This is based on the cerebro-acoustic coherence findings.

claim: Peri-calcarine cortex is functionally connected to areas sensitive to auditory information in temporal cortex.
source: Our results contrast with this view by showing that neuronal populations in (peri-)calcarine cortex align to the temporal dynamics of intelligible speech, and are functionally connected to areas sensitive to auditory information in temporal cortex.
evidence: This is based on the connectivity analysis findings.

claim: In sighted individuals, regions of the temporal lobe including STS are sensitive to acoustic features of speech.
source: In sighted individuals, regions of the temporal lobe including STS are sensitive to acoustic features of speech, whereas higher-level regions such as anterior temporal cortex and left inferior frontal gyrus are relatively insensitive to these features and therefore do not entrain to the syllabic rate of speech (Davis and Johnsrude, 2003; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; see confirmation in Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Davis and Johnsrude (2003) and Hickok and Poeppel (2007), and confirmed by Figure 1F-G.

claim: Higher-level regions such as anterior temporal cortex and left inferior frontal gyrus are relatively insensitive to acoustic features of speech and do not entrain to the syllabic rate of speech.
source: In sighted individuals, regions of the temporal lobe including STS are sensitive to acoustic features of speech, whereas higher-level regions such as anterior temporal cortex and left inferior frontal gyrus are relatively insensitive to these features and therefore do not entrain to the syllabic rate of speech (Davis and Johnsrude, 2003; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; see confirmation in Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Davis and Johnsrude (2003) and Hickok and Poeppel (2007), and confirmed by Figure 1F-G.

claim: Occipital areas respond to speech at a much lower (sensory) level than previously thought in early blind brains.
source: This suggests that occipital areas respond, at least partially, to speech at a much lower (sensory) level than previously thought in EB brains, which may be caused by the reorganization of existing multisensory pathways connecting the 'auditory' and 'visual' centers in the brain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings showing sensory-level processing in occipital cortex.

claim: The sensory-level response in occipital areas may be caused by the reorganization of existing multisensory pathways connecting the 'auditory' and 'visual' centers in the brain.
source: This suggests that occipital areas respond, at least partially, to speech at a much lower (sensory) level than previously thought in EB brains, which may be caused by the reorganization of existing multisensory pathways connecting the 'auditory' and 'visual' centers in the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Functional dependencies between sensory systems exist between the earliest stages of sensory processing in both human and nonhuman primates.
source: Functional dependencies between sensory systems exist between the earliest stages of sensory processing in both human (Ghazanfar and Schroeder, 2006; Kayser et al., 2008; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Murray et al., 2016) and nonhuman primates (Falchier et al., 2002; Lakatos et al., 2007; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several neuroimaging studies have demonstrated enhanced functional connectivity in sighted individuals between auditory and visual cortices under multisensory conditions.
source: Several neuroimaging studies have demonstrated enhanced functional connectivity in sighted individuals between auditory and visual cortices under multisensory conditions (see Murray et al., 2016 for a recent review), including multisensory speech (Giordano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murray et al. (2016) and Giordano et al. (2017).

claim: Neuroimaging studies have shown that hearing people consistently activate left temporal regions during silent speech-reading.
source: Moreover, neuroimaging studies have shown that hearing people consistently activate left temporal regions during silent speech-reading (Calvert et al., 1997; MacSweeney et al., 2000, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Calvert et al. (1997), MacSweeney et al. (2000), and MacSweeney et al. (2001).

claim: Brain networks that are typically dedicated to the integration of audio-visual speech signal might be reorganized in the absence of visual inputs and might lead to an extension of speech tracking in the occipital cortex.
source: We therefore postulate that brain networks that are typically dedicated to the integration of audio-visual speech signal, might be reorganized in the absence of visual inputs and might lead to an extension of speech tracking in the occipital cortex (Collignon et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation to Collignon et al. (2009).

claim: An experience-dependent mechanism related to early blindness affects the strength and directionality of the connectivity between the occipital and temporal regions.
source: Although an experience-dependent mechanism related to EB affects the strength and directionality of the connectivity between the occipital and temporal regions, the presence of intrinsic connectivity between these regions — which can also be observed in sighted individuals (e.g. for multisensory integration) — may constrain the expression of the plasticity observed in our task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the connectivity findings.

claim: The presence of intrinsic connectivity between occipital and temporal regions in sighted individuals may constrain the expression of the plasticity observed in early blind individuals.
source: Although an experience-dependent mechanism related to EB affects the strength and directionality of the connectivity between the occipital and temporal regions, the presence of intrinsic connectivity between these regions — which can also be observed in sighted individuals (e.g. for multisensory integration) — may constrain the expression of the plasticity observed in our task.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Building on connectivity bias, the occipital pole may extend its sensitivity to the intelligibility of speech, a computation this region is not originally dedicated to.
source: Building on this connectivity bias, the occipital pole may extend its sensitivity to the intelligibility of speech, a computation this region is obviously not originally dedicated to.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how plasticity occurs.

claim: Recent studies have suggested that visual deprivation reinforces the functional connections between the occipital cortex and auditory regions typically classified as the language network.
source: A number of recent studies have suggested that visual deprivation reinforces the functional connections between the occipital cortex and auditory regions typically classified as the language network (Hasson et al., 2016; Schepers et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hasson et al. (2016) and Schepers et al. (2012).

claim: Previous studies using dynamic causal modelling support the idea that auditory information reaches the reorganized occipital cortex of the blind through direct temporo-occipital connection.
source: Previous studies using dynamic causal modelling support the idea that auditory information reaches the reorganized occipital cortex of the blind through direct temporo-occipital connection, rather than using subcortical (Klinge et al., 2010) or top-down pathways (Collignon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klinge et al. (2010) and Collignon et al. (2013).

claim: The overall magnitude of functional connectivity between occipital and temporal cortex is higher in blind people than in sighted people during natural speech comprehension.
source: In support of these studies, we observed that the overall magnitude of functional connectivity between occipital and temporal cortex is higher in blind people than in sighted people during natural speech comprehension.
evidence: This is based on the phase-locking value analysis.

claim: Directional connectivity analysis revealed that the interaction between occipital and temporal cortices is qualitatively different between blind and sighted individuals.
source: Moreover, directional connectivity analysis revealed that the interaction between the two cortices is also qualitatively different: sighted individuals show a strong feed-forward drive towards temporal cortex, whereas blind individuals show a more balanced information flow, and a trend in the reverse direction.
evidence: This is based on the phase-slope index analysis.

claim: The changes in connectivity between blind and sighted individuals are not limited to the occipito-temporal network.
source: However, this does not mean that the changes in connectivity between blind and sighted individuals are limited to this specific network (e.g. see Kayser et al., 2015; Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a caveat with citations to Kayser et al. (2015) and Park et al. (2015).

claim: According to the asymmetric sampling in time model, there is a division of labour between the left- and right auditory cortices.
source: According to an influential model of speech comprehension – the asymmetric sampling in time model (AST; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; Poeppel, 2003) – there is a division of labour between the left- and right auditory cortices (Poeppel, 2003; Boemio et al., 2005; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007), with the left auditory cortex being more sensitive to high-frequency information (+20 Hz), whereas the right temporal cortex is more sensitive to low-frequency information (~6 Hz) such as syllable sampling and prosody (Belin et al., 1998; Poeppel, 2003; Boemio et al., 2005; Obleser et al., 2008; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The left auditory cortex is more sensitive to high-frequency information (+20 Hz).
source: According to an influential model of speech comprehension – the asymmetric sampling in time model (AST; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; Poeppel, 2003) – there is a division of labour between the left- and right auditory cortices (Poeppel, 2003; Boemio et al., 2005; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007), with the left auditory cortex being more sensitive to high-frequency information (+20 Hz), whereas the right temporal cortex is more sensitive to low-frequency information (~6 Hz) such as syllable sampling and prosody (Belin et al., 1998; Poeppel, 2003; Boemio et al., 2005; Obleser et al., 2008; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The right temporal cortex is more sensitive to low-frequency information (~6 Hz) such as syllable sampling and prosody.
source: According to an influential model of speech comprehension – the asymmetric sampling in time model (AST; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007; Poeppel, 2003) – there is a division of labour between the left- and right auditory cortices (Poeppel, 2003; Boemio et al., 2005; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007), with the left auditory cortex being more sensitive to high-frequency information (+20 Hz), whereas the right temporal cortex is more sensitive to low-frequency information (~6 Hz) such as syllable sampling and prosody (Belin et al., 1998; Poeppel, 2003; Boemio et al., 2005; Obleser et al., 2008; Giraud and Poeppel, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several studies have shown that the right hemisphere is specifically involved in the representation of connected speech.
source: Several studies have shown that the right hemisphere is specifically involved in the representation of connected speech (Bourguignon et al., 2013; Fonteneau et al., 2015; Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2015; Alexandrou et al., 2017), whereas other studies have directly demonstrated the prevalence of speech-to-brain entrainment while listening to sentences or stories in delta and theta bands in the right hemisphere more than in the left hemisphere (Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Abrams et al., 2008; Gross et al., 2013; Giordano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Other studies have directly demonstrated the prevalence of speech-to-brain entrainment while listening to sentences or stories in delta and theta bands in the right hemisphere more than in the left hemisphere.
source: Several studies have shown that the right hemisphere is specifically involved in the representation of connected speech (Bourguignon et al., 2013; Fonteneau et al., 2015; Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2015; Alexandrou et al., 2017), whereas other studies have directly demonstrated the prevalence of speech-to-brain entrainment while listening to sentences or stories in delta and theta bands in the right hemisphere more than in the left hemisphere (Luo and Poeppel, 2007; Abrams et al., 2008; Gross et al., 2013; Giordano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The present study replicates previous results by showing enhanced phase coupling between the right hemisphere and the speech envelope at the syllabic rate.
source: The present study therefore replicates these results by showing enhanced phase coupling between the right hemisphere and the speech envelope at the syllabic rate (low-frequency phase of speech envelope), consistent with the AST model.
evidence: This is based on the current study's findings in right STG.

claim: Right hemispheric sensitivity to intelligible speech in temporal areas coincides with the enhanced right hemispheric sensitivity to intelligible speech in the occipital cortex of blind individuals.
source: An interesting observation in the current study is that right hemispheric sensitivity to intelligible speech in temporal areas coincides with the enhanced right hemispheric sensitivity to intelligible speech in the occipital cortex of blind individuals.
evidence: This is an observation from the current study's findings.

claim: Blind people have enhanced speech discrimination in noisy environments as compared to sighted individuals.
source: Previous studies have indeed demonstrated that, as compared to sighted individuals, blind people have enhanced speech discrimination in noisy environments (Niemeyer and Starlinger, 1981), as well as the capability to understand speech displayed at a much faster rate (sighted listeners at rates of 9–14 syllables/s andblind listeners at rates of 17–22 syllables/s; Moos and Trouvain, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Niemeyer and Starlinger (1981).

claim: Blind people have the capability to understand speech displayed at a much faster rate than sighted individuals.
source: Previous studies have indeed demonstrated that, as compared to sighted individuals, blind people have enhanced speech discrimination in noisy environments (Niemeyer and Starlinger, 1981), as well as the capability to understand speech displayed at a much faster rate (sighted listeners at rates of 9–14 syllables/s andblind listeners at rates of 17–22 syllables/s; Moos and Trouvain, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moos and Trouvain (2007).

claim: Listening to intelligible ultra-fast speech causes enhanced activity in the right primary visual cortex in early and late blind individuals when compared to sighted controls.
source: Crucially, listening to intelligible ultra-fast speech (as compared to reverse speech) has been shown to cause enhanced activity in the right primary visual cortex in early and late blind individuals when compared to sighted controls, and activity in this region correlates with individual ultra-fast speech perception skills [Dietrich et al., 2013]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dietrich et al., 2013.

claim: Activity in right primary visual cortex correlates with individual ultra-fast speech perception skills in blind individuals.
source: Crucially, listening to intelligible ultra-fast speech (as compared to reverse speech) has been shown to cause enhanced activity in the right primary visual cortex in early and late blind individuals when compared to sighted controls, and activity in this region correlates with individual ultra-fast speech perception skills [Dietrich et al., 2013]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dietrich et al., 2013.

claim: The engagement of right V1 in the analysis of the speech envelope may support the enhanced encoding of early supra-segmental aspects of the speech signal, supporting the ability to understand an ultra-fast speech signal.
source: These results raise the interesting possibility that the engagement of right V1 in the analysis of the speech envelope, as demonstrated in our study, may support the enhanced encoding of early supra-segmental aspects of the speech signal, supporting the ability to understand an ultra-fast speech signal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking the current findings to enhanced speech perception abilities.

claim: The behavioral task in the current study did not allow direct assessment of the link between the reorganized occipital cortex and speech comprehension.
source: However, our behavioral task (speech comprehension) did not allow us to directly assess this link between the reorganized occipital cortex and speech comprehension, as by design performance was almost at ceiling in the nat and 8-chan condition but at chance in the 1-chan condition (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the behavioral design.

claim: Linking brain activity and behavior is not a trivial issue.
source: However, it is important to note that linking brain activity and behavior is not a trivial issue.
evidence: This is a general statement about methodological challenges.

claim: Many studies have not found a direct link between crossmodal reorganization and non-visual processing.
source: Many studies have not found a direct link between crossmodal reorganization and non-visual processing.
evidence: This is a general statement about findings in the field.

claim: A behavioral outcome is the end product of a complex interactive process between several brain regions.
source: More generally, as a behavioral outcome is the end product of a complex interactive process between several brain regions, linking the role of one region in isolation (e.g. the reorganized region in the occipital cortex of blind people) to behavior (e.g. performance) in a multifaced task is not straightforward.
evidence: This is a general statement about the complexity of brain-behavior relationships.

claim: An absence of a direct relation between behavior and crossmodal plasticity could be explained by the fact that complex processes are supported by additional networks other than the reorganized ones.
source: An absence of a direct relation between behavior (e.g. speech processing) and crossmodal plasticity could be explained by the fact that this complex process is supported by additional networks other than the reorganized ones.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of direct brain-behavior correlations.

claim: Early visual deprivation triggers a game of 'balance' between the brain systems typically dedicated to a specific process and the reorganized occipital cortex.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have shown that early visual deprivation triggers a game of 'balance' between the brain systems typically dedicated to a specific process and the reorganized occipital cortex (Dormal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dormal et al. (2016).

claim: Early visual deprivation triggers a redeployment mechanism that would reallocate part of the processing typically implemented in the preserved networks to the occipital cortex deprived of its most salient input.
source: It has indeed been proposed that early visual deprivation triggers a redeployment mechanism that would reallocate part of the processing typically implemented in the preserved networks (i.e. the temporal or frontal cortices for speech processing) to the occipital cortex deprived of its most salient input (vision).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal about the mechanism of reorganization.

claim: Two recent studies using multivoxel pattern analysis showed that the ability to decode different auditory motion stimuli was enhanced in hMT+ of early blind individuals.
source: Two recent studies using multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) showed that the ability to decode the different auditory motion stimuli was enhanced in hMT+ (a region typically involved in visual motion in sighted individuals) of early blind individuals, whereas an enhanced decoding accuracy was observed in the planum temporale in the sighted group (Jiang et al., 2016; Dormal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jiang et al. (2016) and Dormal et al. (2016).

claim: Enhanced decoding accuracy for auditory motion was observed in the planum temporale in the sighted group.
source: Two recent studies using multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) showed that the ability to decode the different auditory motion stimuli was enhanced in hMT+ (a region typically involved in visual motion in sighted individuals) of early blind individuals, whereas an enhanced decoding accuracy was observed in the planum temporale in the sighted group (Jiang et al., 2016; Dormal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jiang et al. (2016) and Dormal et al. (2016).

claim: Bedny et al. (2015) reported an enhanced activation of occipital cortex and a simultaneous deactivation of prefrontal regions during a linguistic task in blind children.
